newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria appoints large team to plan future.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria appoints large team to plan future.

text.p: Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha has named a 172-member group of Nigerians and foreign residents to plan the nation's future under his "Vision 2010" programme.

An official statement in the capital Abuja on Monday said the team, to be inaugurated by Abacha on Wednesday, was led by industrialist Ernest Shonekan, the man from whom Abacha seized power in 1993 during chaos unleashed by the annulment of a presidential election intended to restore democracy.

Members include traditional rulers, editors of three leading independent newspapers, prominent bankers and businessmen and the chief executives in Nigeria of major multinational oil firms such as Mobil, Shell and Elf.
"Their job is to shape the future of this country not only economically but to plan how Nigeria can achieve greatness," said a government spokesman.

Abacha launched "Vision 2010", which is modelled on plans in other countries such as Malaysia, last month. It aims to raise Nigeria's gross domestic product through agriculture and industrialisation as well as improve literacy levels, healthcare and employment.

Brian Anderson, British chief executive of Royal Dutch Shell Group in Nigeria, told a seminar in Lagos this month that for the plan to succeed Nigeria needs investment in oil and gas, the economy's backbone.

"In the world of Vision 2010, the Nigerian oil and gas industry has tremendous potential for growth," said Anderson, who was born in Nigeria. "The potential can only be realised with major investments in the industry."

Another key member of the group is Theo Oerlemans, the Dutch chief executive of Nigeria's liquefied natural gas firm that has a $4 billion project to tap and sell Nigerian gas in Europe and America from 1999.

Oerlemans and Anderson were key to continuing the project when foreign groups pressed for its cancellation because of the government's hanging a year ago of nine minority rights activists, including author Ken Saro-Wiwa.

Nigeria's economy, the biggest in Sub-Saharan Africa outside of South Africa, slumped into recession after the election annulment but policies since 1995 have stabilised it and the government has promised measures in next year's budget to revive growth.
